18:  * @method addUIInterruptionMonitorWithDescription:handler:
19:  *
20:  * @abstract Adds a monitor to the test. Monitors are automatically removed at the end of the test or can be manually removed using -removeUIInterruptionMonitor:.
21:  * Monitors are invoked in the reverse order in which they are added until one of the monitors returns true, indicating that it has handled the interruption.
22:  *
23:  * @param handlerDescription
24:  * Explanation of the behavior and purpose of this monitor, mainly used for debugging and analysis.
25:  *
26:  * @param handler
27:  * Handler block for asynchronous, non-deterministic interrupting UI such as alerts and other dialogs. Handlers should return true if they handled the UI, false if they did not.
28:  * The handler is passed an XCUIElement representing the top level UI element for the alert.
29:  *
30:  * @return Returns an opaque token that can be used to remove the monitor.
31:  *
32:  * @discussion
33:  * A "UI interruption" is any element which unexpectedly blocks access to an element with which a UI test is trying to interact. Interrupting elements are most commonly alerts,
34:  * dialogs, or other windows, but can be of other types as well. Interruptions are unexpected or at least not deterministic: the appearance of an alert in direct response to
35:  * a test action such as clicking a button is not an interruption and should not be handled using a UI interruption monitor. Instead, it's simply part of the UI and should be
36:  * found using standard queries and interacted with using standard event methods. Note that some interruptions are part of the app's own UI, others are presented on
37:  * behalf of system apps and services, so queries for these elements must be constructed with the right process at their root.
38:  *
39:  * Use a UI interruption monitor for alerts that appear unexpectedly or with non-deterministic timing. Monitors are not invoked simply by the appearance of an alert or similar
40:  * UI, they are called when the presence of such UI interferes with actions the test is attempting to take. For example, consider the following sequence:
41:  *
42:  * - test taps button
43:  * - app displays confirmation dialog
44:  *
45:  * In this case, the dialog that is presented can be anticipated by the test, so a UI interruption monitor should not be used. Instead, the sequence should look like:
46:  *
47:  * - test taps button
48:  * - test constructs an XCUIElement for the dialog and uses XCUIElement.waitForExistence(timeout:) to wait for it to appear
49:  * - app displays confirmation dialog
50:  * - test synthesizes a tap for the appropriate button in the dialog
51:  * - test continues execution
52:  *
53:  * There was no UI interruption in this example because every step was deterministic and known in advance. Note the use of XCUIElement.waitForExistence(timeout:) to deal with
54:  * asynchronous delays in the display of the dialog.
55:  *
56:  * By contrast, consider the next sequence, where use of a UI interruption monitor is the correct solution:
57:  *
58:  * - test launches app
59:  * - app initiates asynchronous network request
60:  * - test interacts with app
61:  * - network request completes, app decides to display a dialog to the user
62:  * - dialog appears just as the test is about to tap on a button
63:  *      - the appearance of the dialog is not deterministic
64:  *      - the test can anticipate that the dialog might be displayed at some point, but not when
65:  *      - accordingly, the test has installed a UI interruption monitor that knows how to handle the network response dialog
66:  * - when XCTest computes a hit point for the button, it discovers the dialog and treats it as "interrupting UI"
67:  * - the previously installed UI interruption monitor is invoked
68:  * - it handles the dialog
69:  * - XCTest computes the hit point for the button and synthesizes the requested tap event
70:  * - test execution continues...
71:  *
72:  * Monitors can be designed to be general or specific in how they handle interruptions. The simplest general approach might simply attempt to cancel/dismiss/close
73:  * any interrupting dialog/alert/window without consideration for its contents or purpose. A more specific monitor might make decisions based on the UI and contents
74:  * of the interruption. Tests may install multiple monitors, which will be invoked in reverse order of installation. If a more specific monitor wishes to be skipped for a
75:  * given interruption, its handler can simply return false - the next monitor will be invoked, and so on, until one of them returns true, signifying that it has handled
